title: Hello, I'm Ani
title_target: გამარჯობა, მე ანი ვარ — Gamarjoba, me Ani var
goal: Greet Georgians the right way, say who you are, ask other people's names, and say goodbye properly — all with a single verb.

dialogs.title: დიალოგი — First day of class
dialogs.intro: Ani, a student from Indonesia, has just arrived in Tbilisi and today is her first Georgian class. At the door she meets Nino. Notice that the greeting and its reply are two different words — a habit English doesn't share.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: His name is Giorgi. He's very nice.

notes: **გამარჯობა doesn't literally mean "hello" — it means "victory to you".** The greeting is a relic of wartime: returning soldiers were welcomed with a wish for victory. The reply is not the same word again but **გაგიმარჯოს** — "may victory be yours". ⚠️ This is the first trap for English speakers, who answer "hello" with "hello". Answering გამარჯობა with გამარჯობა isn't wrong and people will understand, but გაგიმარჯოს instantly sounds like someone who has really studied.

**There is no separate word for "am/is/are" — it's built into the verb.** მე ვარ = "I am". The interesting part: the subject can be dropped entirely. *ანი ვარ* alone already means "I'm Ani", because the **ვ-** at the front of the verb already says the subject is "I". You will meet that ვ- prefix on almost every verb in this course.

**არის often shrinks to -ა and sticks to the word before it.** მასწავლებელი + არის → მასწავლებელ**ია**. კარგი + არის → კარგ**ია**. The long form is still correct (ის მასწავლებელი არის), but everyday speech almost always uses the short one.

**რა გქვია? literally means "what is called to you", not "who is your name".** ⚠️ Learners are often tempted to use ვინ (who) here. Georgian uses **რა** (what) — just like English "what's your name?". ვინ ხარ? means "who are you, anyway?" and sounds like an interrogation.

**კარგად, not კარგი.** კარგი = good (adjective), კარგად = well (adverb). The ending **-ად** turns adjectives into adverbs, like English -ly, and it comes back in unit 3 with a bigger job: ქართულ**ად** = "in Georgian".
**მეც = მე + ც.** The particle **-ც** means "too / also" and always sticks to the end of a word, never standing alone. შენ**ც** (you too), ის**ც** (he/she too), დღეს**ც** (today too).

**Two ways to say goodbye, depending on who is leaving.** The person **leaving** says ნახვამდის (until we meet). The person **staying** answers კარგად (be well). If both are heading off in different directions, both can say კარგად.

grammars.title: ვარ, ხარ, არის — your first and most-used verb
body: The only form you need to learn by heart today. Notice that the pronouns (მე, შენ, ის) are in brackets: they can be there or not — the verb already carries that information.

rows: მასწავლებელი ხართ? — are you a teacher?

after: ⚠️ **თქვენ ხართ** has two uses: "you" (several people) and polite "you" (one person, formal). With anyone you've just met, especially someone older, use თქვენ. Switching to შენ is usually offered later by the other person.

grammars.title: Asking and giving names
body: There are two ways to give your name, and both are equally common. The second is easier for beginners because it's built just like English "my name is".
after: Watch the changing prefix: **მ**ქვია (to me), **გ**ქვია (to you), **ჰ**ქვია (to him/her). This მ-/გ-/ჰ- set comes back in unit 4 with the verb "to have", and in unit 16 with the verb "to hurt". It's a small group of verbs, but you'll use them every day.

sections.title: Time-of-day greetings, and five lifesaver phrases

blocks.text: გამარჯობა works any time, morning to night. But time-of-day greetings sound warmer, and all three follow the same pattern: the time of day + მშვიდობისა ("peace").

blocks.title: Five phrases that will save your first day
items: **მადლობა** (madloba) — thank you. The polite version is **გმადლობთ** (gmadlobt). The reply is **არაფრის** (arapris, "it's nothing").
**ბოდიში** (bodishi) — sorry, when you've done something wrong. **უკაცრავად** (uk'atsravad) — excuse me, when you want to interrupt or ask a stranger something.
**ვერ გავიგე** (ver gavige) — I didn't catch that; please repeat. The most useful sentence of your first week.
**ქართული ცოტა ვიცი** (kartuli tsot'a vitsi) — I know a little Georgian. Say this and the other person will slow down.

blocks.text: One small note to save you some awkwardness: Georgians almost never treat a mispronunciation as a problem. What they value isn't your fluency but the fact that you're trying at all. *ქართული ცოტა ვიცი* usually earns far more praise than you deserve — just accept it with a მადლობა.
